title: What a project is
blurb: Define a project the APM way and spot the hallmarks that make a piece of work a project.
question: Hartwell Primary School asks a small team to design and build an outdoor classroom, hand it over to the teachers before September, and then go back to their usual jobs. Is this a project, and which features of the work make it one?

teach.body: A new hospital wing, an office move, a product launch, a village fete: each one is a project. Organisations use projects whenever they need something to change. This first lesson gives you the APM definition of a project, the foundation for the whole PFQ. Every later topic (life cycles, roles, planning, risk) assumes you can tell a project from other work, so it is worth getting rock solid now.

APM defines a project as a unique, transient endeavour undertaken to bring about change and to achieve planned objectives. In plain English: a one-off piece of work, with a start and a finish, that changes something and has clear goals. 'Transient' simply means temporary. The project exists only until its objectives are met, then it closes and its team moves on.

teach.h: Unpacking the definition, phrase by phrase

children.label: Unique
children.sub: Not done in exactly this way before

children.label: Transient endeavour
children.sub: Temporary: a defined start and finish

teach.caption: Four phrases, four ideas. Exam options that describe work as ongoing, routine or repeatable are describing something that is NOT a project.

teach.h: The six hallmarks, applied to Hartwell's outdoor classroom
head: Hallmark
What it means
Hartwell example
rows: A one-off: never done exactly like this
This site, this design, this school
Starts in April, done by September
Lessons can now be taught outdoors
Funded and staffed for this work
teach.caption: Check any piece of work against these six. If it is one-off, time-bound and changes something, you are looking at a project.

teach.h: A project has a beginning and an end

items.label: Need agreed
items.sub: Governors approve the idea and a budget

items.label: Temporary team formed
items.sub: Head teacher, builder, governor and a project manager

items.label: Handed over
items.sub: Teachers take ownership of the new space

items.label: Project closes
items.sub: Team disbands; using the classroom is now routine

teach.caption: The project ends, but what it delivered lives on. Teaching in the classroom every week is not the project: that is everyday work.

teach.body: A project's planned objectives are usually expressed as what it will deliver and why. The OUTPUT is the thing produced (the outdoor classroom). The OUTCOME is the change that results (lessons taught outside). The BENEFIT is the measurable improvement people value (better pupil engagement). Projects produce outputs; the change and benefits are the reason they are worth doing. You will meet benefits again in the Planning topic.

steps.label: Output
steps.sub: What the project produces: the outdoor classroom

steps.label: Outcome
steps.sub: The change it enables: lessons held outdoors

steps.label: Benefit
steps.sub: The measurable gain: higher pupil engagement

teach.caption: Objectives can be stated as outputs, outcomes or benefits. All three point to change.

rows.label: No school has this exact design and site
Must be handed over before September
Pupils will learn in a new way
A wet May could delay the groundworks

teach.note: Uncertainty comes with uniqueness: because the work is new, nobody can be sure exactly how it will go, which is why projects need risk management.

teach.text: 'Temporary' describes the PROJECT, not what it produces. A bridge may last 100 years, but the project to build it ends at handover. And size is irrelevant: a small one-off job can be a project, while a huge but repetitive operation is not.

teach.h: Your PFQ exam at a glance

items.label: marks lost for a wrong answer, so answer everything

teach.caption: Every learning outcome is examined, including this one. Learn the definitions closely: the exam rewards precise wording.

items: A project is a unique, transient endeavour undertaken to bring about change and to achieve planned objectives.
Transient means temporary: a defined start and finish, then the team disbands.
Hallmarks: unique, temporary, delivers change, defined objectives, its own budget and team, uncertainty.
Ongoing, routine or repeatable work is not a project, however big or important it is.

summary: You can now give the APM definition of a project and recognise its hallmarks: unique, temporary, change-making, objective-driven, with its own team and budget and some uncertainty. You can also explain why the project ends even when its outputs last for years.

A.q: Complete the statement: a project is a unique, transient endeavour undertaken to…
options: sustain the organisation's ongoing routine operations
bring about change and achieve planned objectives
coordinate several related pieces of change work
balance investment across the whole organisation
A.why: The APM definition ends: undertaken to bring about change and to achieve planned objectives.

whyNot.0: Sustaining routine operations describes business as usual, which is ongoing rather than transient.
whyNot.2: Coordinating related pieces of change work describes programme management.
whyNot.3: Balancing investment across the organisation describes portfolio management.

A.q: In the APM definition of a project, what does the word 'transient' mean?
options: Temporary
Complex
Low risk
Repeatable
A.why: Transient means temporary: the project has a defined start and finish and exists only until its objectives are met.

whyNot.1: Projects are often complex, but that is not what 'transient' means.
whyNot.2: Projects carry uncertainty because they are unique, so they are not defined as low risk.
whyNot.3: Repeatable work is the opposite of a project; it describes business as usual.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT a hallmark of a project?
options: A defined start and a defined finish
A unique set of outputs to deliver
A team that stays together for good
An element of risk and uncertainty
A.why: Projects use a temporary team that disbands when the work is done. A permanent team is a feature of business as usual.

whyNot.0: A defined start and finish is exactly what 'transient' means, so it is a hallmark.
whyNot.1: Uniqueness is a core hallmark: the work has not been done in exactly this way before.
whyNot.3: Because projects are unique, they always carry some uncertainty (risk).

B.q: Which of the following pieces of work is a project?
options: Restocking a shop's shelves every night
Answering calls on an IT helpdesk daily
Running the monthly payroll for staff
Opening the first branch in a new city
B.why: Opening a first branch in a new city is one-off, time-bound and brings about change, so it is a project.

whyNot.0: Nightly restocking is repetitive, ongoing work: business as usual.
whyNot.1: A daily helpdesk is a continuing service, not a temporary endeavour.
whyNot.2: Monthly payroll repeats on a cycle with no end point, so it is business as usual.

B.q: Why do projects usually carry more uncertainty than routine work?
options: Their work has not been done in this way before
Their teams are always less experienced than others
They are never given a budget until they finish
They always involve new technology of some kind
B.why: Uniqueness creates uncertainty: with no exact precedent, nobody can be sure how the work will turn out.

whyNot.1: Project teams can be very experienced; uncertainty comes from the work being new, not the people.
whyNot.2: Projects have their own budget from the start, so this is false.
whyNot.3: Many projects involve no new technology at all, such as an office move or a charity event.

B.q: A council builds a footbridge expected to last 80 years. Which statement is correct?
options: It is not a project, because the bridge is permanent
It is not a project, because councils run services
It is a project only if it takes longer than a year
It is a project, because building it is temporary
B.why: 'Temporary' applies to the endeavour, not the output. The building work starts and finishes, so it is a project even though the bridge lasts decades.

whyNot.0: The permanence of the output does not matter; the work to create it is still temporary.
whyNot.1: Councils run services (business as usual) and also run projects; who does the work is not the test.
whyNot.2: There is no minimum duration. A project can last weeks or years.

C.q: A bakery makes the same 500 loaves every morning. It then designs a one-off cake for a royal visit next month. Which statement is correct?
options: The loaves and the cake are both projects
The cake is a project; the loaves are not
The loaves are a project; the cake is not
Neither is a project, as both are baking
C.why: The royal cake is unique, time-bound and has a specific objective, so it is a project. The daily loaves are repetitive, ongoing work.

whyNot.0: The daily loaves repeat every morning with no end point, so they are not a project.
whyNot.2: This reverses the two: repetition marks the loaves as routine, and uniqueness marks the cake as a project.
whyNot.3: The type of activity is not the test. A one-off, time-bound piece of baking with set objectives is a project.

C.q:
Which TWO of the following are hallmarks of a project?
1) It delivers change
2) It repeats on a regular cycle
3) It has planned objectives
4) It continues with no set end
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
C.why: Projects bring about change (1) and achieve planned objectives (3). Both phrases come straight from the APM definition.

whyNot.0: Item 2 (repeating on a regular cycle) describes business as usual, not a project.
whyNot.1: Items 2 and 4 both describe ongoing, routine work: the opposite of a project.
whyNot.3: Item 4 is wrong: a project is transient, with a defined finish.

C.q: A project manager says: 'Our project is done once the new warehouse opens, even though it will run for 20 years.' Which part of the project definition is she applying?
options: That a project is transient
That a project is low risk
That a project is repetitive
That a project is permanent
C.why: She recognises the project is transient: it ends at handover. Running the warehouse afterwards is ongoing work, not the project.

whyNot.1: Projects carry uncertainty; nothing in her statement concerns risk.
whyNot.2: Projects are unique, not repetitive. Repetitive work is business as usual.
whyNot.3: The warehouse is long-lasting, but the project is not permanent: that is her whole point.

reteach.title: Think of a wedding
reteach.question: Planning a wedding is a classic project. Married life afterwards is not. What is the difference, and how does it map to the APM definition?

blocks.body: A wedding is unique (this couple, this venue, this date). It is transient: planning starts with the engagement and ends after the big day. It brings about change: two people are now married. It has planned objectives: the guest list, the budget, the date. A temporary 'team' (planner, caterer, florist, best friend) forms for it and then disbands. And there is uncertainty: will it rain?

blocks.caption: The project delivers the change; ongoing life (in organisations, business as usual) carries it forward.

blocks.text: Big and important does not mean 'project'. A hospital's daily operating theatre list is huge and vital, but it is routine work. Building a new theatre is the project.

explain.body: A project has not been done in exactly this way before: a new site, a new design, a new combination of people or constraints. Even if a firm has built 50 houses, the 51st on a different plot, for a different client, is still a unique piece of work.

test.q: Which word in the APM definition of a project captures that the work has not been done in exactly that way before?
options: Transient
Unique
Endeavour
Objective
test.why: Unique means one-off: not done in exactly this way before.

whyNot.0: Transient means temporary, with a start and a finish.
whyNot.2: Endeavour simply means an undertaking or effort.
whyNot.3: Objectives are the goals the project must achieve.

explain.body: A project is temporary. It has a defined start and a defined finish, and a temporary team that is formed for the work and released when it ends. When the objectives are met (or the project is stopped), it closes.

test.q: What happens to a project team once the project's objectives are achieved?
options: It runs the outputs as a service
It becomes a permanent department team
It is disbanded and people move on
It starts the same project again
test.why: Project teams are temporary: they disband when the project closes and members return to other work.

whyNot.0: Running outputs as an ongoing service is business as usual, usually done by the operational teams.
whyNot.1: A permanent department is the opposite of a transient project organisation.
whyNot.3: Projects are unique; repeating the same work would be routine, not a project.

explain.body: Projects exist to move an organisation from how things are now to how it wants them to be. If nothing is different afterwards, there was no reason to run a project. This is why projects are often called the vehicles for change.

test.q: According to the APM definition, a project is undertaken mainly to…
options: keep current operations stable
use up the annual change budget
keep specialist staff fully busy
bring about change in some way
test.why: The APM definition says a project is undertaken to bring about change and achieve planned objectives.

whyNot.0: Keeping operations stable is the aim of business as usual, not projects.
whyNot.1: Spending a budget is never the purpose of a project.
whyNot.2: Keeping staff busy is not a reason to run a project; delivering change is.

explain.body: A project has clear, agreed objectives from the start: what it will deliver and what it is for. They can be expressed as outputs (the things produced), outcomes (the change) or benefits (the measurable improvement). Clear objectives tell everyone when the project is finished and whether it succeeded.

test.q: In which terms are a project's planned objectives usually expressed?
options: Outputs, outcomes and benefits
Teams, roles and departments
Shares, dividends and profits
Policies, rules and procedures
test.why: Project objectives describe what will be delivered and why: outputs, the outcomes they enable, and the benefits that follow.

whyNot.1: Teams and roles describe how the work is organised, not what it must achieve.
whyNot.2: Financial returns may feature in a business case, but objectives are framed as outputs, outcomes and benefits.
whyNot.3: Policies and procedures govern routine work; they are not project objectives.
